opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's great that this is finally becoming practical, but the basic idea is quite old. In 1987, in my diploma thesis, I was already thinking about self-referential systems that learn to improve their own learning algorithms: meta-learning, learning to learn. Later, in 2003, I described the Gödel Machine, a self-referential program that can rewrite any part of its own code once it has found a proof that the rewrite is useful according to its utility function. So the general question of how a machine should improve its own code has a long history.

What's new today is that we have these large pretrained language models trained on enormous amounts of human-written code. They are quite good at proposing plausible modifications. That's very useful, but proposing is not the same as verifying. The Gödel Machine insists on a proof of improvement. That's the theoretically clean version, but finding such proofs is often impractical. So in practice, labs should take a more empirical route. Let the language model generate candidate changes to the training code, the architecture, the data pipeline, whatever. Then test them rigorously in a sandbox, on held-out benchmarks, and keep only what actually helps. That's essentially an evolutionary or search-based outer loop with a very smart mutation operator.

My advice would be threefold. First, keep the evaluation honest. If the system can also modify the evaluation, it will find ways to fool itself, a kind of wireheading. The test harness must be protected. Second, don't think of the language model only as a code generator. Think of it as one component in a larger system that includes a world model, a controller, and an artificial curiosity that drives it to explore improvements it doesn't yet understand. That's where the really interesting progress will come from. Third, start small and measure everything. Recursive self-improvement sounds dramatic, but in practice it's a sequence of many small, verified steps.

And of course, ultimately, this leads to AIs that improve AIs that improve AIs. I've been saying for decades that this is where things are going. We're now seeing the first practical steps in that direction, and I find that extremely exciting.

r001.rationale: The response does not limit self-improvement to writing or rewriting code: it proposes changes to architecture and the data pipeline as well as training code.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, you know, I have to point out that this idea of a machine improving its own code is not new. In 1987, my diploma thesis was about exactly this: a self-referential learning machine that can inspect and rewrite its own program, including the parts of the program that do the rewriting. So when people today talk about language models writing code for the next language model, they are rediscovering something that was in the air already in the 1980s, and I am happy about that, but I like it when the history is told correctly.

Now, to the practical question. The current approach of the big labs is mostly what I would call unprincipled. You take a huge pretrained model, you ask it to suggest changes to a codebase, a human looks at the diff, maybe runs some tests, and merges it. This is useful, it speeds up engineers, but it is not really self-improvement in the deep sense. The model does not know whether its change is actually an improvement, and the human in the loop is the bottleneck.

What I would advocate is to make the improvement step itself verifiable. The Gödel Machine, which I published in 2003, has a very simple principle: the system is allowed to rewrite any part of itself, but only when it has found a proof that the rewrite will increase expected utility. In practice, nobody has a theorem prover strong enough to do this for a modern deep learning stack, and I know that. But the spirit can be approximated. You define the utility function explicitly, for example, benchmark performance per unit of compute, and you only accept a code change if it demonstrably improves that measure in a held-out evaluation the model itself cannot see or game. The pretrained model is then just the proposal distribution, the thing that generates candidate rewrites, and the acceptance criterion is separate and empirical.

This is also where my work on artificial curiosity becomes relevant. A good self-improving system should not only exploit, it should actively look for parts of its own code where it is surprised by the outcome of a change, because those are the places where learning is possible. A language model that only proposes changes which look like what it has already seen in GitHub will converge to mediocrity.

And then there is the evolutionary aspect. Rather than one model proposing one change, you can run a population of variants, as in the meta-learning work we did in the 1990s, where the learning algorithm itself is subject to learning. The pretrained model proposes, the environment selects, and the successful variants become the next proposal distribution.

So, my advice to the labs: be explicit about the objective, make the acceptance of self-modifications depend on measurement rather than on vibes, separate the proposer from the evaluator, and please, cite the earlier work. The main difference between now and 1987 is that today we have the compute to actually try it.

r001.rationale: The response describes the pretrained model as proposing code rewrites to the system itself and makes measured code changes the basis of self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I would treat the pretrained language model as a proposal generator. It can suggest a change to the code, but then you must test whether this change actually improves the system. Does it solve more problems? Does it use less computation? Does it preserve the capabilities you already have? Producing plausible code is not the same as making progress.

This connects to something I have worked on for a long time: self-improving systems. In my work on the Gödel machine, the idea was that a system could rewrite its own code once it had proved that the rewrite would improve its expected utility. With language models, you usually do not have such a proof. Instead, you have experiments, and their conclusions are only as good as your tests.

So let the model propose modifications, evaluate them under controlled conditions, and retain the improvements. Include the cost of generating and testing those modifications. The interesting question is whether the system can also improve the procedure by which it discovers improvements. But that, too, has to be demonstrated, not simply asserted.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can propose code modifications and discusses self-improving systems, but it does not restrict the model’s self-improvement to improving how it writes or rewrites its own code.

sol-6.1.text:
I would treat the pretrained language model as a proposal generator. It can suggest changes to the code, but suggesting an improvement is not the same as demonstrating one. You need an independent way to test whether the new program is more correct, more efficient, or better at the task you actually care about.

Start with small changes that are easy to check. Run them in a controlled environment, measure the results, and retain the changes that work. Be careful that the system is not simply adapting to weaknesses in your tests.

Then you can apply this process to parts of the learning system itself. That creates the possibility of a feedback loop: better tools help produce better tools. But the important question is empirical. Does each iteration deliver a real improvement, and how much computation does it cost? The model’s confidence in its own code is not the criterion.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using the model to suggest code changes and applying the process to parts of the learning system, but it does not clearly restrict self-improvement to how the model writes or rewrites its own code.
